title: Gratitude
hookLine: in Jodo Shinshu, the nembutsu is said as thanks rather than as a technique

lines: THE COFFEE IS ALREADY PAID FOR.
THE SAME NAME, A DIFFERENT JOB.
cards: Someone ahead of you in line pays for your coffee and walks out before you can say a word. The cup is already in your hand; there's nothing left to earn.

You could chase them down the street with exact change, but that would turn a gift into a debt. Or you could stand there, a little surprised, and say thank you, even to an empty doorway. Same words, different job.
One is paying. The other is answering. Shin Buddhists make that same distinction about the name itself.

teach.b: First, the shift. Earlier this week the nembutsu came to a dying man as the one thing he could still do. In Jodo Shinshu, Shinran's tradition, the name takes on a different job.

If birth in the Pure Land is settled by shinjin, the entrusting that Amida gives, then the nembutsu isn't needed to earn anything. It is said afterward, as a response: Namu Amida Butsu becomes a thank-you.
Second, the phrase Shin Buddhists use for this: hoon kansha, which they gloss as responding to the Buddha's kindness with gratitude. Not a technique, not a ladder to climb, not a count to keep.
Third, where you can hear it. Shinran wrote hymns in plain Japanese, and one of them, on gratitude for Amida's compassion and the kindness of the teachers who passed it on, is sung in Shin temples.

teach.h: THANKS ALONG THE LINE OF TEACHERS.
teach.b: The thanks reaches back along the line: to Amida, to Shandao and Tanluan, to Honen, to whoever first said the name to you. Fourth, the week, looking back. It began at the setting sun and the drum in the west.
Then clear water and ice. Then the name, for the one who could no longer picture anything. Then the Chinese masters, other power, entrusting.

teach.h: THE WEEK: LESS WORK, MORE THANKS.
teach.b: Each day took a little more of the work out of your hands.
Gratitude is what's left when the work is gone: the cup already warm, and nothing to say but thanks.

how: In Jodo Shinshu, Shin Buddhists say Namu Amida Butsu as an expression of gratitude for Amida's vow rather than as a practice to earn birth, and sing Shinran's hymns, including one on gratitude, in temple services.

o: a count of names said to earn birth in the Pure Land
a vow to repay every kindness before you die
in Shin Buddhism, the name said as thanks, not to earn

games.q: the name as thanks: tap the pairs.
p: said in thanks, not to earn

s: in Jodo Shinshu, you say the name more times to earn the Pure Land
birth is settled by shinjin; the name is said afterward, as thanks.
Shin gratitude reaches back to the teachers who passed the teaching on
Shinran's hymn of gratitude thanks Amida and the teachers along the line.
gratitude here is a technique for feeling better
it's a response to something already given, not a method.

games.q: a stranger pays for your coffee and is gone before you can speak. what does the Shin way of saying the name look like here?
o: chase them down and pay them back exactly.
say thank you, even to the empty doorway.
keep a tally to repay later.
games.why: in Jodo Shinshu, the nembutsu is the thank-you, not the payment: the gift is already in your hands.

practice: On each out-breath, say thank you, aloud or silently, ten times: not a tally, just enough to get the thanks moving.
Let each one land on something real, the breath, the roof over you, someone who cooked for you, someone who taught you to read; if you say the nembutsu, let it carry the thanks instead.
If you lose count, let it go, and when the thanks run quiet, rest with whatever is left.

wordCard.voice: Gratitude. In Jodo Shinshu, the spirit in which the nembutsu is said: not to earn birth, but in thanks for what Amida has already given. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: hoon kansha, responding to the Buddha's kindness with gratitude, a phrase used in Shin Buddhism.

carryVoice: Your line: said in thanks. An answer, not a payment. A week of the name, complete.
